title: Part 1, Chapter 5
paragraphs: "Of course, I've been meaning to go see Razumikhin, to ask him about work, to get him to find me some tutoring or something..." Raskolnikov thought. "But what can he do for me now? Say he finds me lessons, say he shares his last kopeck with me -- if he has one -- so I can buy boots and make myself presentable enough to give lessons... hmm... and then what? What am I going to do with a few kopecks? That's not what I need now. It's really absurd to be going to Razumikhin...."
The question of why he was heading to Razumikhin's now troubled him more than he realized. He kept searching uneasily for some hidden meaning in this seemingly ordinary action.
"Did I really think I could fix everything, find a way out, just by going to Razumikhin?" he asked himself in confusion.
He thought hard, rubbing his forehead. Then, strangely, after a long stretch of brooding, a thought came to him -- suddenly, as if by accident, as if of its own accord.

"Hmm... to Razumikhin's," he said all at once, calmly, as though he had reached a final decision. "I'll go to Razumikhin's, of course, but... not now. I'll go to him... the day after It, when It is done and everything begins again...."
And suddenly he realized what he was thinking.

"After It!" he shouted, jumping up from the bench. "But is It really going to happen? Is it possible that it actually will?" He left the bench and broke into a near-run. He meant to turn back toward home, but the thought of going home suddenly filled him with violent revulsion. In that hole, in that awful little closet, all of _this_ had been growing inside him for the past month. He walked on aimlessly.

His nervous shuddering had turned into a fever that left him shivering. Despite the heat, he felt cold. With a kind of desperate effort, he began staring at every object he passed, almost unconsciously, driven by some inner need for distraction. But it didn't work, and he kept sinking back into dark thoughts. Whenever he would startle and look up, he immediately forgot what he'd just been thinking and where he was going. In this way he walked all the way across Vasilyevsky Island, came out onto the Lesser Neva, crossed the bridge, and turned toward the islands. At first the greenery and freshness were soothing to his exhausted eyes after the dust of the city and the massive buildings that crowded in on him and weighed him down. There were no taverns here, no suffocating closeness, no stench. But soon even these pleasant new sensations turned into a morbid irritability. Sometimes he stopped in front of a brightly painted summer villa set among green foliage. He would gaze through the fence at elegantly dressed women on verandas and balconies, at children running in the gardens. The flowers especially caught his attention -- he stared at them longer than at anything. He also passed luxurious carriages and men and women on horseback. He watched them with curious eyes but forgot about them before they were out of sight. At one point he stopped and counted his money. He had thirty kopecks. "Twenty to the policeman, three to Nastasya for the letter, so I must have given forty-seven or fifty to the Marmeladovs yesterday," he calculated, for no particular reason, but soon forgot why he had taken the money out at all. He remembered when he passed a tavern, and realized he was hungry.... He went in, drank a glass of vodka, and ate some kind of pie, finishing it as he walked. It had been a long time since he'd had vodka, and it hit him immediately, even though he'd only had one small glass. His legs suddenly grew heavy and a powerful drowsiness came over him. He headed home, but when he reached Petrovsky Island, he stopped, completely spent, turned off the road into the bushes, sank down on the grass, and fell asleep instantly.

In a fevered state, dreams often have a strange realism, a vividness and extraordinary likeness to reality. The images created can be monstrous, yet the setting and the entire picture are so lifelike, so filled with details so subtle, so unexpected yet so artistically perfect, that the dreamer himself, even if he were an artist like Pushkin or Turgenev, could never have invented them while awake. Such feverish dreams stay in the memory for a long time and make a powerful impression on an already strained and destabilized nervous system.

Raskolnikov had a terrible dream. He dreamed he was back in his childhood, in the small town where he was born. He was a boy of about seven, walking through the countryside with his father on the evening of a holiday. It was an overcast, heavy day, and the landscape was exactly as he remembered it -- in fact, he saw it far more vividly in the dream than he ever had in memory. The small town sat on a flat, open plain, bare as the palm of a hand, without even a willow tree nearby. Only in the far distance, a dark smudge of woods showed at the very edge of the horizon. A few steps beyond the last vegetable garden stood a tavern, a large tavern, which had always filled him with aversion, even fear, when he walked past it with his father. There was always a crowd there -- shouting, laughter, cursing, ugly hoarse singing, and often fighting. Drunk, terrifying-looking men hung around outside. He would press close to his father, trembling, whenever he saw them. Near the tavern, the road turned to a dusty track, and the dust was always black. The road wound on, and about a hundred paces further it curved right toward the cemetery. In the middle of the cemetery stood a stone church with a green dome where he used to go to services two or three times a year with his mother and father, for memorial masses for his grandmother, who had died long ago and whom he had never known. On those occasions they would bring a white dish wrapped in a napkin, filled with a special rice pudding with raisins pressed into it in the shape of a cross. He loved that church, with its plain, old-fashioned icons, and the old priest with the trembling head. Near his grandmother's grave, which was marked by a stone, was the tiny grave of his younger brother, who had died at six months old. He didn't remember him at all, but he had been told about his little brother, and every time he visited the cemetery he would cross himself solemnly, bow down, and kiss the small grave. Now he dreamed he was walking with his father past the tavern on the way to the cemetery, holding his father's hand and looking at the tavern with dread. Something unusual was going on. There seemed to be some kind of celebration: a crowd of townspeople in their best clothes, peasant women, their husbands, and riffraff of every sort, all singing and all more or less drunk. Near the entrance to the tavern stood a cart -- but a strange cart. It was one of those large carts usually pulled by heavy draft horses, piled high with wine barrels or other heavy loads. He had always loved watching those massive horses, with their long manes, thick legs, and slow, steady pace, pulling enormous loads with no apparent effort, as though carrying a load were easier for them than going empty. But now, strangely, a thin little sorrel nag had been harnessed to this huge cart. It was one of those peasant horses he had often seen straining desperately under heavy loads of wood or hay, especially when the wheels got stuck in the mud or in a rut. The peasants would beat them so cruelly, sometimes even across the nose and eyes, and he felt so sorry, so sorry for them that he nearly cried, and his mother always pulled him away from the window. Suddenly there was an eruption of shouting, singing, and balalaika music, and a group of large, very drunk peasants came pouring out of the tavern, wearing red and blue shirts with coats slung over their shoulders.
"Get in, everybody get in!" shouted one of them -- a young, thick-necked peasant with a fleshy face as red as a beet. "I'll take you all! Get in!"
But immediately the crowd burst into laughter and jeering.
"Take us all with a horse like that!"
"Mikolka, you're crazy! Hitching a nag like that to a cart like this?"
"That mare's twenty years old if she's a day, boys!"

"Get in! I'll take you all!" Mikolka shouted again, leaping into the cart first, grabbing the reins, and standing up straight at the front. "The bay went off with Matvey," he shouted from the cart, "and this old wreck is breaking my heart -- I feel like I could kill her. She just eats and eats and does nothing. Get in, I said! I'll make her gallop! She'll gallop!" He snatched up the whip, eagerly preparing to flog the little mare.
"Get in! Come on!" The crowd laughed. "You hear that -- she'll gallop!"
"Gallop! She hasn't galloped in ten years!"
"She'll manage a trot!"
"Never mind her, boys -- grab a whip each, get ready!"
"Right! Let her have it!"

They all scrambled into Mikolka's cart, laughing and joking. Six men piled in and there was still room. They hauled in a plump, rosy-cheeked woman dressed in red cotton, wearing a beaded pointed headdress and thick leather shoes. She was cracking nuts and laughing. The crowd around them laughed too -- and how could they not? This wretched nag was supposed to pull the whole cartload of them at a gallop! Two young fellows in the cart had already gotten their whips ready to help Mikolka. With a cry of "Now!" the mare strained with all her might, but far from galloping, she could barely move. She struggled with her legs, panting and flinching under the three whips that rained down on her like hail. The laughter in the cart and the crowd doubled, but Mikolka flew into a rage and beat the mare furiously, as though he actually believed she could gallop.
"Let me in too, boys!" yelled a young man in the crowd, excited by the spectacle.
"Get in, everybody get in!" Mikolka screamed. "She'll pull you all! I'll beat her to death!" And he lashed and lashed at the mare, beside himself with fury.
"Papa, Papa!" the boy cried. "Papa, what are they doing? Papa, they're beating the poor horse!"

"Come along, come along!" his father said. "They're drunk, they're being stupid, they're just fooling around. Come away, don't look!" He tried to pull him away, but the boy tore free from his hand and ran to the horse, beside himself with horror. The poor animal was in a bad way. She was gasping, standing still, then lurching forward again, nearly falling.
"Beat her to death!" Mikolka screamed. "That's what it's come to! I'll finish her!"
"What are you doing? Are you even a Christian, you devil?" an old man in the crowd shouted.
"Who ever heard of a wretched nag like that pulling such a load?" said another.
"You'll kill her!" shouted a third.
"Don't meddle! She's my property! I'll do as I please! Get in, more of you! Everyone get in! I'll make her gallop!..."

Suddenly the crowd roared with laughter, drowning out everything. The mare, stung by the hail of blows, had begun feebly kicking. Even the old man couldn't help smiling. A pathetic little animal like that, trying to kick!
Two boys in the crowd snatched up whips and ran to the mare to beat her ribs -- one on each side.
"Hit her in the face! In the eyes! In the eyes!" Mikolka screamed.
"Give us a song, boys!" someone shouted from the cart, and everyone in it launched into a rowdy song, jingling a tambourine and whistling. The woman went on cracking nuts and laughing.

...The boy ran alongside the mare, ran out in front of her, watched them whipping her across the eyes, right in the eyes! He was crying, choking, tears streaming down his face. One of the men lashed him across the face with a whip. He didn't feel it. Wringing his hands and screaming, he rushed to the gray-haired old man with the gray beard who was shaking his head in disapproval. A woman grabbed the boy by the hand and tried to pull him away, but he tore free and ran back to the mare. She was nearly finished but tried to kick one more time.

"I'll teach you to kick!" Mikolka roared. He threw down the whip, bent forward, and pulled a long, thick wooden shaft from the bottom of the cart. He gripped one end with both hands and, with great effort, swung it over the mare.
"He'll crush her!" voices shouted around him. "He'll kill her!"
"She's my property!" Mikolka screamed, and brought the shaft crashing down. There was the sound of a heavy thud.
"Hit her! Hit her! Why'd you stop?" voices yelled from the crowd.

Mikolka swung the shaft a second time, and it came down again on the spine of the wretched mare. Her hindquarters buckled, but she lurched forward, straining with everything she had -- pulling one way, then the other, trying to move the cart. But six whips were attacking her from every direction, and the shaft rose and fell on her a third time, then a fourth, in heavy, measured blows. Mikolka was in a frenzy because he couldn't kill her with a single blow.
"Tough one!" someone shouted in the crowd.
"She'll go down any second now, boys. She's nearly done," said an admiring spectator.
"Bring an axe! Finish her off!" shouted a third.

"I'll show you! Stand back!" Mikolka screamed. He flung down the shaft, bent into the cart, and pulled out an iron crowbar. "Watch this!" he bellowed, and with all his strength brought it smashing down on the mare. The blow landed. The mare staggered, sank back, tried to pull forward, but the bar came down again in a savage arc across her back and she collapsed to the ground like a felled tree.

"Finish her off!" Mikolka screamed, and leaped out of the cart, wild-eyed. Several young men, also flushed with drink, grabbed whatever they could find -- whips, sticks, poles -- and ran to the dying mare. Mikolka stood to one side, raining random blows with the crowbar. The mare stretched out her head, drew one long breath, and died.
"You butchered her!" someone in the crowd shouted.
"Why wouldn't she gallop, then?"
"My property!" Mikolka yelled, standing with bloodshot eyes, brandishing the crowbar. He looked as though he regretted having nothing left to beat.
"That's no Christian, that's for certain!" many voices were shouting in the crowd.

But the poor boy, beside himself, fought his way through the crowd to the sorrel mare, threw his arms around her bleeding dead head, and kissed it -- kissed her eyes, kissed her lips.... Then he leapt up and flew at Mikolka in a frenzy, swinging his small fists. At that instant his father, who had been chasing after him, snatched him up and carried him out of the crowd.
"Come along, come along! Let's go home," his father said.
"Papa! Why did they... kill... the poor horse!" he sobbed, but his voice broke and the words came in shrieks from his heaving chest.

"They're drunk.... They're brutes... it's not our business!" his father said. The boy threw his arms around his father but felt choked, suffocating. He tried to draw a breath, tried to cry out -- and woke up.
He woke gasping for breath, drenched in sweat, and sat up in terror.
"Thank God, it was only a dream," he said, sitting down under a tree and taking deep breaths. "But what is this? Am I coming down with a fever? What a horrifying dream!"
He felt completely shattered. Darkness and confusion filled his soul. He rested his elbows on his knees and buried his face in his hands.

"My God!" he cried. "Can it be -- can it really be -- that I'm going to take an axe, that I'm going to hit her on the head, split her skull open... that I'm going to step in the warm, sticky blood, break the lock, steal, and tremble -- hide myself, covered in blood... with the axe.... My God, can it be?"
He was shaking like a leaf as he said this.

"But why do I keep going over this?" he continued, sitting up again as if in profound amazement. "I knew I could never bring myself to do it, so why have I been torturing myself all this time? Yesterday, when I went to do that... _experiment_ -- yesterday I realized completely that I could never go through with it.... So why am I going over it again? Why am I still hesitating? Coming down the stairs yesterday, I told myself it was base, loathsome, vile, vile... the very thought of it made me sick, filled me with horror.

"No, I can't do it. I can't! Granted, there is no flaw in the reasoning. Granted, everything I've concluded over the past month is clear as day, true as mathematics.... But my God! I can't bring myself to do it! I can't! So why, why am I still...?"

He rose to his feet, looked around in wonder as though surprised to find himself here, and started walking toward the bridge. He was pale, his eyes were burning, he was exhausted in every limb -- but he suddenly seemed to breathe more easily. He felt he had thrown off the terrible weight that had been pressing down on him for so long. All at once a feeling of relief and peace settled over his soul. "Lord," he prayed, "show me my path. I renounce that cursed... dream."

Crossing the bridge, he gazed quietly and calmly at the Neva, at the blazing red sun setting in the blazing sky. Despite his weakness, he felt no fatigue. It was as though an abscess that had been forming in his heart for a month had suddenly burst. Freedom, freedom! He was free of that spell, that sorcery, that obsession!

Later, when he looked back on that time and everything that happened to him in those days -- minute by minute, point by point -- he was struck by one circumstance with almost superstitious force. Though not extraordinary in itself, it always seemed to him afterward to be the predestined turning point of his fate. He could never understand or explain to himself why, when he was exhausted and it would have been far more convenient to go straight home by the shortest route, he had instead gone through the Hay Market, where he had no reason to go. The detour was obvious and completely unnecessary, though not a long one. True, it had happened to him dozens of times to walk home without noticing which streets he took. But why -- he kept asking himself -- why had such an important, such a decisive, and at the same time such a completely chance encounter happened in the Hay Market (where he had no business being) at the very hour, the very minute of his life when he was in exactly the state of mind and exactly the circumstances in which that encounter could exert the gravest and most decisive influence on his entire destiny? As though it had been lying in wait for him on purpose!

It was about nine o'clock when he crossed the Hay Market. At the tables and stalls, the booths and shops, all the vendors were closing up, clearing away, and packing their goods, and like their customers, heading home. Ragpickers and peddlers of every kind crowded around the taverns in the dirty, stinking courtyards of the Hay Market. Raskolnikov particularly liked this area and the surrounding alleys when he wandered the streets aimlessly. Here his rags drew no contemptuous stares, and you could walk around in any condition without shocking anyone. At the corner of an alley, a peddler and his wife had two tables set up selling ribbon, thread, cotton handkerchiefs, and the like. They had gotten up to leave but were lingering in conversation with a woman who had just approached them. This woman was Lizaveta Ivanovna -- or, as everyone called her, Lizaveta -- the younger sister of the old pawnbroker, Alyona Ivanovna, whom Raskolnikov had visited the day before to pawn his watch and conduct his _experiment_.... He already knew all about Lizaveta, and she knew him slightly too. She was a single woman of about thirty-five, tall, clumsy, timid, meek, and almost simple-minded. She was a complete slave to her sister, who made her work day and night and even beat her. She was standing in front of the peddlers with a bundle, listening earnestly and doubtfully. They were talking about something with particular intensity. The moment Raskolnikov caught sight of her, he was overcome by a strange feeling, something like intense astonishment, though there was nothing especially surprising about the encounter.
"You should make up your own mind, Lizaveta Ivanovna," the peddler was saying loudly. "Come by tomorrow around seven. They'll be there too."
"Tomorrow?" Lizaveta said slowly and thoughtfully, as though unable to decide.

"Honestly, the way you're terrified of Alyona Ivanovna!" the peddler's wife chattered -- a lively little woman. "I look at you and you're like a little child. And she's not even your real sister -- just a half-sister. And the control she has over you!"

"But this time don't say a word to Alyona Ivanovna," her husband cut in. "That's my advice. Just come to us without asking her. It'll be worth your while. Your sister can figure things out for herself later."
"Should I come?"
"Around seven tomorrow. And they'll be here. You can decide for yourself."
"And we'll have a cup of tea," his wife added.
"All right, I'll come," Lizaveta said, still pondering, and slowly started to move away.

Raskolnikov had just passed by and heard every word. He walked on softly, unnoticed, trying not to miss anything. His initial astonishment gave way to a thrill of horror, like a shiver running down his spine. He had learned -- suddenly, completely unexpectedly -- that tomorrow at seven o'clock, Lizaveta, the old woman's sister and only companion, would be away from home, and that therefore at precisely seven o'clock the old woman _would be completely alone_.

He was only a few steps from his lodging. He walked in like a man condemned to death. He thought of nothing and was incapable of thinking. But he felt suddenly, with his whole being, that he no longer had any freedom of thought, any will -- and that everything had been suddenly and irrevocably decided.

Certainly, if he had waited whole years for a suitable opportunity, he could not have hoped for a more certain step toward the success of his plan than the one that had just presented itself. In any case, it would have been difficult to discover beforehand, with such certainty, such precision, and so little risk -- without dangerous inquiries or investigations -- that the next day, at a specific hour, the old woman whose life he was contemplating would be home and entirely alone.
